explanations.explanation: Isaiah says, "When you have finished destroying, you will be destroyed." The destroyer has been dishing it out, and now it comes back around to him. The traitor gets the same treatment: "you will be betrayed." I think that guy never once pictured the line turning around.

That's not what the verse says. When the destroyer finishes destroying, Isaiah says "you will be destroyed." Nobody gets a forever throne out of that sentence. The one lifted up in this chapter is the LORD, who "dwells on high" (Isaiah 33:5).

Forgiveness isn't what this verse hands the destroyer. What he gets is "you will be destroyed." Forgiveness does show up later in the chapter, but it's for the people who live in Zion (Isaiah 33:24). So this one isn't about him.

Close, but the prayer asks for more than that. It says, "Be our strength every morning and our salvation in time of trouble." So strength is asked for every single morning, not just on the rough days. Trouble gets its own request, which is salvation.

Right, friend. The prayer says, "Be our strength every morning and our salvation in time of trouble." Strength is for every morning, even the quiet ones. Salvation is the part that's asked for in time of trouble.

The verse says, "the nations scatter when You rise." Just before that, "The peoples flee the thunder of Your voice." So when the LORD stands up, everybody else is on the move, and not toward Him. I'd scatter too.
Not here. The prayer says "the peoples flee the thunder of Your voice." Standing firm would mean staying put, and these nations don't. When the LORD rises, they scatter.

The verse goes the other direction. It says "the nations scatter when You rise." Scattering means moving away, and the peoples flee at the thunder of His voice. Nobody in this verse is walking closer.

That's it. "He has filled Zion with justice and righteousness." The LORD is exalted because He dwells on high, and what He puts into Zion is justice and righteousness. That's what He fills the city with.
Nice guess, but the verse doesn't mention gold or silver. It says the LORD "has filled Zion with justice and righteousness." Those are what He fills the city with.
No chariots in this verse, friend, and no horses either. Isaiah says the LORD "has filled Zion with justice and righteousness." The next verse even calls the LORD the "sure foundation," not an army.

Yes, ma'am, yes, sir! "The fear of the LORD is Zion's treasure." Right before that, He's called "a storehouse of salvation, wisdom, and knowledge." So the treasure Isaiah names isn't something you can count.
Isaiah doesn't go there. He says, "The fear of the LORD is Zion's treasure." No gold is mentioned in the verse. The storehouse he names holds "salvation, wisdom, and knowledge."

Walls would be a fair guess for a city, but Isaiah doesn't say that. He says, "The fear of the LORD is Zion's treasure." The LORD Himself is called the "sure foundation for your times." So the treasure here is the fear of the LORD, not stone.

That's the verse: "the envoys of peace weep bitterly." These are the very people sent to make peace, and they're in tears. Right alongside them, the valiant ones cry aloud in the streets. It's a hard scene, and I think it hurts to read.
The verse doesn't say they leave. It says "the envoys of peace weep bitterly." Fleeing is what the peoples do at the LORD's voice (Isaiah 33:3). These envoys are weeping.
Isaiah doesn't put them indoors. He says, "the envoys of peace weep bitterly." The valiant ones are out in the streets crying aloud. So the envoys' weeping is what the text gives us.
Yes. Isaiah says, "The treaty has been broken." The same verse says the highways are deserted and travel has ceased. A broken treaty means a promise nobody kept.
It actually is in there. Verse 8 says, "The treaty has been broken, the witnesses are despised, and human life is disregarded." That comes right after the empty highways. So Isaiah does say it.
That's right. "The witnesses are despised." The people who should be listened to when a treaty falls apart are the ones getting looked down on. The verse adds that "human life is disregarded."
It's the opposite. Isaiah says, "the witnesses are despised." Nobody is handing out rewards in this verse. The treaty is broken, and human life is disregarded.
The verse doesn't say they're missing. It says "the witnesses are despised." They're still around, and people look down on them. That's the picture Isaiah paints.

Yes, "Bashan and Carmel shake off their leaves." Bashan and Carmel are places in the land, and here they're dropping leaves as the land mourns. The same verse says Sharon is like a desert. It's a sad picture of a land that's worn out.

Nice try, but blossoms aren't what the verse names. Isaiah says Bashan and Carmel "shake off their leaves." Blossoms would be a prettier picture, and this one isn't pretty. The land mourns and languishes.
Fruit isn't in this verse. It says Bashan and Carmel "shake off their leaves." Leaves falling fits a land that mourns and languishes. Sharon is described as being like a desert in the same verse.
That's the word: "Now." The LORD says, "Now I will arise," and then, "Now I will lift Myself up. Now I will be exalted." He says it three times in a row. I'd say He means it.
The LORD doesn't say later. He says, "Now I will arise," and then repeats "Now" twice more. That's three "Now"s in a row.
No harvest in this verse, friend. The LORD says, "Now I will arise." Then He says, "Now I will lift Myself up. Now I will be exalted." It's all "Now."

Yes. "Your breath is a fire that will consume you." The ones who conceive chaff and give birth to stubble get burned by their own breath. It's a hard verse. Nobody else lights it, since it's their own breath.
A warm fire would be nice, but this one isn't. The LORD says, "Your breath is a fire that will consume you." Consume means it burns them up. Chaff and stubble don't make a cozy blaze.
This fire doesn't lead anybody anywhere. The LORD says, "Your breath is a fire that will consume you." A fire that consumes burns things up. Chaff and stubble are what go into it.
Yes. The LORD says, "The peoples will be burned to ashes, like thorns cut down and set ablaze." Thorns cut down go up fast, and the comparison stays on that picture. It's a serious verse.
It is in there. The LORD says, "The peoples will be burned to ashes, like thorns cut down and set ablaze." It follows the line about chaff and stubble. So the statement is true.

Close, but there's more to it. The LORD says, "You who are far off, hear what I have done; you who are near, acknowledge My might." So the call goes out to those far off and those near. Nobody gets left out of this one.
Yes. The LORD says, "You who are far off, hear what I have done; you who are near, acknowledge My might." He calls the far off and the near. So it's for everybody.

explanations.answer: Who can dwell with everlasting flames
explanations.explanation: That's the question. "Who of us can dwell with a consuming fire? Who of us can dwell with everlasting flames?" The sinners in Zion are afraid, and trembling grips the ungodly. It's a question that comes out of fear.

explanations.answer: When the enemy will finally leave
explanations.explanation: That isn't what they ask. They ask, "Who of us can dwell with a consuming fire? Who of us can dwell with everlasting flames?" Nothing in the verse mentions an enemy leaving. Their question is about the fire.

explanations.answer: Where the nearest city of refuge is
explanations.explanation: No cities of refuge here, friend. The ungodly ask, "Who of us can dwell with a consuming fire? Who of us can dwell with everlasting flames?" Trembling grips them, and the question is about the flames.
Yes. This person is described as one "whose hand never takes a bribe." He also "refuses gain from extortion." His hands stay clean.
The verse says the opposite. The one who walks righteously is the one "whose hand never takes a bribe." He also "refuses gain from extortion." So the statement is true.

explanations.answer: He stops his ears against them
explanations.explanation: That's what the verse says: "who stops his ears against murderous plots." He also "shuts his eyes tightly against evil." He won't listen and he won't look.

explanations.answer: He reports them to the elders
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say that. It says he is one "who stops his ears against murderous plots." No elders show up in it. Stopping his ears is what Isaiah gives us.

explanations.answer: He warns the city about them
explanations.explanation: That's a good guess, but it isn't in the text. Isaiah says he "stops his ears against murderous plots." He also "shuts his eyes tightly against evil." So the verse stays with his ears and eyes.
Yes. "The mountain fortress will be his refuge." He'll dwell on the heights, and a fortress up there is where he's safe. That sounds a lot better than a leaky tent.
Close to the idea, but not what's said. Isaiah says, "the mountain fortress will be his refuge." No cave is mentioned. A fortress is what he gets.
A tent isn't named for this man. Isaiah says, "the mountain fortress will be his refuge." Tents do come up later in the chapter, but for Jerusalem (Isaiah 33:20). Here it's a fortress.
Not quite. Isaiah says, "his food will be provided and his water assured." That means he doesn't have to worry about it. It's taken care of.
Yes. The text says, "his food will be provided and his water assured." Provided and assured mean he won't be sweating it. A fortress and a full table, all in one verse.
That's the promise. "Your eyes will see the King in His beauty." Isaiah is talking about seeing the King with your own eyes. And he adds a land that stretches afar.
No priest here. Isaiah says, "Your eyes will see the King in His beauty." He's talking about the King.
That's a good thought, but it isn't what Isaiah says. He says, "Your eyes will see the King in His beauty." It's the King who is in view.
Yes. Isaiah says they will "behold a land that stretches afar." That comes right after seeing the King in His beauty. A whole wide land, in view.
It is in the verse. Isaiah says, "Your eyes will see the King in His beauty and behold a land that stretches afar." So the land comes along with the King.
Isaiah says the opposite. He says, "You will no longer see the insolent, a people whose speech is unintelligible." No longer means they're gone from view. So they won't be dealing with them.

That's it. Isaiah says, "You will no longer see the insolent, a people whose speech is unintelligible, who stammer in a language you cannot understand." No longer means no more. They'll be gone from sight.
Yes. Jerusalem is "a tent that does not wander." Its tent pegs won't be pulled up, and its cords won't be broken. This tent stays put.
Shining isn't in this verse. It says Jerusalem is "a tent that does not wander." The pegs and cords are what keep it in place.
Nothing about opening here. Isaiah says Jerusalem is "a tent that does not wander." Its pegs won't be pulled up and its cords won't be broken.
Yes. "The Majestic One, our LORD, will be for us a place of rivers and wide canals." The place isn't a king or a city on its own. The LORD Himself is that place for them.
Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, isn't named in this passage. Isaiah says, "the Majestic One, our LORD, will be for us a place of rivers and wide canals." The LORD is the one he points to.
David, Israel's king, isn't named here. Isaiah says, "the Majestic One, our LORD, will be for us a place of rivers and wide canals." The LORD is the one named.
Yes. "It is He who will save us." The LORD is their Judge, their lawgiver and their King, and He's the one who saves. That's the end of the verse.
Testing isn't what the verse says. It says, "It is He who will save us." Judge, lawgiver and King all lead to that one line.
Watching isn't in this verse. Isaiah says, "It is He who will save us." The LORD saves them.
That's what Isaiah says: "even the lame will carry off plunder." The spoils are so abundant that even someone who can't move fast gets a share. Everybody walks away with something.
Elders aren't mentioned. Isaiah says, "even the lame will carry off plunder." The lame are the ones he names.
Strangers don't show up in that verse. Isaiah says, "even the lame will carry off plunder." The lame are the ones named.
Yes. "The people who dwell there will be forgiven of iniquity." That's how the chapter ends. And right before it, no resident of Zion will say, "I am sick."
That isn't what Isaiah says. He says, "The people who dwell there will be forgiven of iniquity." Forgiven is where the chapter lands.
That's not in the verse. Isaiah says, "The people who dwell there will be forgiven of iniquity." Forgiven is what happens to it.
